issues.topic: A 20-minute money reset for the new year
issues.subject: Your 20-minute money reset for 2027
issues.preheader: Three checks that pay off all year, starting with your paycheck.
issues.headline: A 20-minute money reset for the new year
explain: New year, new plan year. Before January gets busy, take 20 minutes for three checks. None of them need a budget app or a spreadsheet, and each one keeps working for you all year.
The idea is simple: decide once, then let automatic transfers do the work. Money you never see in your checking account is money you don't have to resist spending.
issues.tell: Decide once, automate it, and stop relying on willpower.
steps: **Check your {{RETIREMENT_PLAN}} contribution** in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}}. {{MATCH_LINE}} If you're putting in less than the match, you're leaving part of your pay on the table.
**Set up one automatic transfer** to savings on payday, even $25. Name the account "Emergency fund". A common first goal is $1,000, then one month of essential bills.
**Pull your free credit reports** at [AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com), typed in yourself. They're free every week, and checking your own credit never lowers your score.
quick_hits: **Your benefits elections took effect January 1.** Look at your first paycheck of the year and make sure the deductions match what you picked.
**Free trials:** when you sign up for one, set a reminder to cancel the same day.
issues.job: Open your first 2027 pay stub and find three numbers: take-home pay, your {{RETIREMENT_PLAN}} contribution, and your health plan deduction. If any look wrong, contact {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}} this week.

social.caption: New year, 20-minute money reset: 1) Check your {{RETIREMENT_PLAN}} contribution in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}}. 2) Set up an automatic transfer to savings on payday, even $25. 3) Pull your free credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com. Questions about your benefits? Contact {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.
social.alt: Money Made Simple at Work: your 20-minute money reset. Check your retirement contribution. Automate $25 a payday to savings. Pull your free credit reports.

brief.Don't: Recommend specific funds, accounts or amounts, or ask anyone what they earn or save.

issues.topic: Tax season: your W-2, your withholding and side income
issues.subject: Your W-2 is here. Three tax checks worth 15 minutes
issues.preheader: Check your withholding, plan for side income, and skip the IRS text scam.
issues.headline: Tax season, minus the surprises
explain: Your W-2 should arrive by the end of January. Before you file, three quick checks can save you from a surprise bill next year, or a refund that's much smaller than you expected.
Tax rules changed for 2025 and 2026, so last year's habits may not fit this year. The IRS updated its free withholding estimator to include the changes.
issues.tell: Your withholding is a choice you can change any time, and side income needs its own tax plan.
steps: **Run the IRS [Tax Withholding Estimator](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/tax-withholding-estimator)** once you've filed or have your W-2. If it says to change your W-4, update it in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}}.

**Earn money on the side** (rideshare, freelancing, reselling)? No tax is taken out of that money. A common rule of thumb is to set aside 25 to 30% of what you earn on the side, and the IRS may expect [estimated tax payments](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/estimated-taxes) during the year.
**File for free if you can.** Check the IRS's free filing options at IRS.gov before you pay for software.
quick_hits: **The IRS doesn't text or email you out of the blue** about refunds or your account. Delete those messages and type IRS.gov yourself.
**Payroll will never ask** you to confirm your direct deposit details through a link in an email. If you get one, report it to {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.
issues.job: Find your W-2 (paper or in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}}) and put it in one folder with any 1099 forms. Everything in one place is half the work of filing.

social.caption: Tax season checklist: run the free IRS Tax Withholding Estimator, update your W-4 in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}} if it says to, and if you earn money on the side, set some aside for taxes. One more thing: the IRS doesn't text you about refunds. Questions? Contact {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.
social.alt: Money Made Simple at Work: tax season, minus the surprises. Run the IRS withholding estimator. Side income? Set some aside. The IRS isn't texting you.

brief.If someone asks a tax question: "I'm not a tax adviser. The IRS estimator is free, and a tax professional can help with your situation."
brief.Escalate: Any email asking an employee to change direct deposit through a link: forward it to IT and {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}} the same day.

issues.topic: What actually moves your credit score
issues.subject: 5 credit score myths, and what actually moves it
issues.preheader: Checking your score doesn't hurt it. Here's what does.
issues.headline: What actually moves your credit score
explain: Your credit score affects more than loans. It can change what you pay for car insurance, whether you need a deposit for utilities, and what a landlord thinks of your application.
A lot of what people believe about credit scores is wrong. Checking your own score doesn't lower it. Your income isn't part of it. And a high balance hurts only while it's high.
issues.tell: Pay on time, keep card balances low compared with your limits, and check your reports for mistakes.
steps: **Set up autopay for at least the minimum** on every card and loan. Late payments are the single biggest drag on a score, and they can stay on your report for years.
**Pay the statement balance in full** if you can. You'll pay $0 interest on purchases, and lower balances help your score.
**Check your free credit reports** at [AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com) and dispute anything that isn't yours with the credit bureau.
quick_hits: **Your report and your score aren't the same thing.** The report is the record; the score is a number calculated from it.
**A credit freeze is free** at each of the three bureaus. It stops new accounts being opened in your name, and you can lift it when you need credit.
issues.job: Turn on autopay for the minimum payment on every card you have. It takes about 2 minutes a card.

lobby.headline: Checking your score never lowers it.

social.caption: Credit score myth: checking your own score lowers it. It doesn't. What actually moves it: paying on time (set up autopay for at least the minimum), keeping card balances low compared with your limits, and fixing mistakes on your free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com.
social.alt: Money Made Simple at Work: checking your score never lowers it. Autopay at least the minimum. Keep card balances low. Freezing your credit is free.

brief.Don't: Ask about anyone's credit, or recommend a lender, card or credit repair company.

issues.subject: Financial Literacy Month: your {{RETIREMENT_PLAN}} in 10 minutes
issues.preheader: The Rule of 72, the fee that's easy to miss, and what not to do when you change jobs.
issues.headline: Your {{RETIREMENT_PLAN}} in 10 minutes
explain: April is Financial Literacy Month, so here's the shortest useful guide to your retirement plan. You don't need to pick investments today. You just need to know three things.

**The Rule of 72:** divide 72 by a yearly growth rate to see roughly how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, about 12 years. At 8%, about 9. That's why starting early matters more than starting big.
issues.tell: Time does most of the work. Start, keep going, and don't cash out early.
steps: **Log in to {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}}** and check three things: what you contribute, what the match is, and how your money is invested. {{MATCH_LINE}}
**Look at the fees.** Your plan sends a fee disclosure each year. Small percentages add up over decades, so it's worth a look.
**Changing jobs one day?** Ask for a direct rollover into your new plan or an IRA instead of cashing out. Cashing out early usually means taxes and, often, a penalty.
quick_hits: **Add 1% when you get a raise.** You won't miss money you never got used to.

**Try a free calculator:** the SEC's [compound interest calculator](https://www.investor.gov/financial-tools-calculators/calculators/compound-interest-calculator) shows what steady saving can grow to.
issues.job: Find your plan's beneficiary page in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}} and check that the right person is named. It's the most-skipped step in retirement planning.

lobby.headline: Your retirement plan in 10 minutes.
bullets: Changing jobs? Roll it over, don't cash out.

social.caption: April is Financial Literacy Month. Spend 10 minutes on your {{RETIREMENT_PLAN}}: check your contribution and the match, look at the fees, and make sure your beneficiary is up to date. Changing jobs one day? Roll it over instead of cashing out. Log in at {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}}.
social.alt: Money Made Simple at Work: your retirement plan in 10 minutes. Check your contribution and match. Look at the fees. Changing jobs? Roll it over, don't cash out.

brief.Don't: Suggest funds, allocations or contribution amounts. That's investment advice, and it isn't ours to give.

issues.source: MMS evergreen: 'Start a starter emergency fund', 'Automate the boring part'
issues.subject: A $500 cushion changes more than you'd think
issues.preheader: Why a small emergency fund beats a big plan you never start, and how to automate it.
issues.headline: Start a small emergency fund
explain: A surprise bill, a car repair or a vet visit is often what pushes people onto a credit card or a payday loan. A small cushion breaks that chain.
You don't need three months of expenses to start. A first goal of $500, saved a little at a time, covers a lot of the surprises that cause the most stress.
issues.tell: Small and automatic beats big and someday. Start with a first goal you can reach.
steps: **Pick a first goal**, like $500, and give it its own savings account so it isn't mixed with spending money.
**Automate it.** Ask payroll if your pay can be split between two accounts, or set an automatic transfer for payday. {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}} can help with direct deposit.
**Refill it after you use it.** That's what it's for.
quick_hits: **Tax refund or bonus?** Putting part of it in the cushion gets you there fast.
**Struggling right now?** {{EAP_LINE}}
issues.job: Open or rename a savings account "Emergencies only" and set up one automatic transfer, even $10 a payday.

lobby.headline: Start with $500.
bullets: Refill it after you use it.

social.caption: This month: a starter emergency fund. You don't need months of savings to begin. Pick a first goal like $500, give it its own account, and automate a little each payday. Questions about splitting your direct deposit? Contact {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.
social.alt: Money Made Simple at Work: start with $500. Give it its own account. Automate it on payday. Refill it after you use it.

brief.Say in your team huddle: "This month's 10-minute task is one automatic transfer to savings. Even $10 a payday counts."
brief.If someone asks how much they should sav: "There's no right number for everyone. The newsletter suggests a first goal of $500. A financial professional can help with a bigger plan."
brief.Don't: Ask anyone how much they have saved, or suggest specific products or banks.

issues.topic: Summer spending and the subscription audit
issues.subject: The $14.99 you forgot about
issues.preheader: A 15-minute subscription audit, and the 30-day list for summer impulse buys.
issues.headline: Find the subscriptions you forgot about
explain: Free trials that turn into monthly charges, streaming services you stopped watching, apps that renew every year: they're easy to forget because they're small.
Summer adds its own pressure: trips, kids home from school, sales everywhere. Two habits help without making you give anything up.
issues.tell: Small charges you don't notice add up to real money. Look once, cancel what you don't use.
steps: **Do a subscription audit.** Scroll through the last two months of your bank and card statements and list every repeating charge.
**Cancel what you don't use**, and turn off auto-renew on anything you only want for a while.
**Try the 30-day list** for non-essential buys: write it down, and if you still want it in 30 days, buy it.
quick_hits: **Free trial?** Put the end date in your phone the day you sign up.
**Your phone keeps a list too:** the subscriptions page in your app store shows what renews and when.
issues.job: Open your bank or card app and search for the word "subscription" or "monthly". Cancel one you don't use.

social.caption: This month: the subscription audit. Look at two months of statements, list every repeating charge, and cancel the ones you don't use. For summer impulse buys, try the 30-day list. Questions about your benefits? Contact {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.

issues.source: MMS evergreen: 'Avalanche vs snowball', carousel #21 (pay down debt)
issues.topic: Paying down debt: avalanche or snowball
issues.subject: Two ways to pay off debt, and how to pick one
issues.preheader: The avalanche saves the most interest. The snowball keeps you going. Either beats waiting.
issues.headline: Avalanche or snowball?
explain: If you have more than one debt, you'll pay off all of them faster with a plan than by spreading extra money around. There are two common plans.

**The avalanche:** pay the minimum on everything, and put every extra dollar on the debt with the highest interest rate. It saves the most money. **The snowball:** put the extra on the smallest balance first. You get quick wins, which helps many people keep going.
issues.tell: The best plan is the one you'll stick with. Always pay at least the minimum on every debt.
steps: **List your debts** with the balance, the interest rate and the minimum payment.
**Pick avalanche or snowball**, and choose one debt to put extra money on.
**When one is paid off,** move its payment to the next one. That's the part that speeds up.
quick_hits: **Be careful with offers to "settle" your debt for a fee up front.** That's often a scam. A nonprofit credit counselor is a safer place to start.
**Feeling buried?** {{EAP_LINE}}
issues.job: Write your debts on one page, smallest to largest and highest rate to lowest. Circle the one you'll pay extra on.

lobby.headline: Pick one debt and attack it.
bullets: Avalanche saves money; snowball keeps you going.
Roll each payment into the next.

social.caption: This month: paying down debt. The avalanche puts extra money on the highest interest rate first and saves the most. The snowball starts with the smallest balance for quick wins. Pick one, pay the minimum on the rest, and roll each payment into the next. {{EAP_LINE}}
social.alt: Money Made Simple at Work: pick one debt and attack it. List every debt. Avalanche saves money, snowball keeps you going. Roll each payment into the next.

brief.Don't: Recommend a lender, a debt relief company, or borrowing from the retirement plan.

issues.headline: Your mid-year paycheck checkup
explain: Halfway through the year is a good time to check that the right amount of tax is coming out of your pay. A big life change, like marriage, a new baby, a second job or side income, can throw it off.
The IRS has a free online Tax Withholding Estimator. With your latest pay stub, it tells you whether to change your W-4.
issues.tell: Fix your withholding in August, not in April. A small change now can avoid a big bill later.
steps: **Grab your latest pay stub** and run the IRS [Tax Withholding Estimator](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/tax-withholding-estimator).
**Need to change it?** Submit a new W-4 in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}} or ask {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.
**Check your credit reports too.** They're free every week at [AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com), the official site.
quick_hits: **Side income?** You may need to raise withholding or make estimated payments.
**Wrong item on a credit report?** You can dispute it with the credit bureau for free.
issues.job: Run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator with this month's pay stub. It takes about 15 minutes.

social.caption: This month: a mid-year paycheck checkup. Run the free IRS Tax Withholding Estimator with your latest pay stub, and update your W-4 in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}} if it says to. Your credit reports are free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com.

issues.source: Scam Decoded small-business blocks (fake invoices) and newsletter coverage of payroll direct-deposit phishing
issues.subject: The email that asks you to "update your direct deposit"
issues.preheader: Fake HR emails, fake invoices and fake job offers: one habit stops all three.
issues.headline: The scams that come to work
explain: Scammers send emails that look like they're from HR or payroll: "Update your direct deposit before Friday's payroll." The link goes to a fake sign-in page, and the next paycheck goes to the scammer.
Others send past-due invoices for things nobody ordered, or texts offering a remote job that asks you to deposit a check and send part of it back.
issues.tell: Any message that changes where money goes, and is in a hurry, gets checked with a person you already know.
steps: **Never change direct deposit from an email link.** Go to {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}} yourself, or ask {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.
**Match every invoice** to a real order before it's paid, and follow the approval steps even if it says "final notice".
**Report it** to your IT or security team, and at [ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov).
quick_hits: **Job offer that sends you a check** and asks you to send some back? That's a fake check scam.
**Clicked or shared a password?** Tell IT right away. Fast is better than perfect.
issues.job: Find out who to tell at work if you click a bad link, and save their contact in your phone.

lobby.headline: Changing where money goes? Check with a person.
bullets: Never update direct deposit from a link.

social.caption: This month: scams that target employees. A fake HR email asks you to update your direct deposit, and the next paycheck goes to a scammer. Never change payroll details from an email link. Go to {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}} yourself, or contact {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.
social.alt: Money Made Simple at Work: changing where money goes? Check with a person. Never update direct deposit from a link. Match invoices to real orders. Report it fast.

brief.Say in your team huddle: "Payroll will never ask you to update direct deposit through an email link. If you see one, forward it to IT."
brief.If someone asks whether an email is real: "When in doubt, don't click. Go to the portal yourself or call HR on a number you already have."
brief.Don't: Embarrass anyone who clicked. Fast reporting matters more.

issues.source: MMS evergreen: 'HSA vs FSA in one minute', open enrollment checklist
issues.subject: Open enrollment: 5 things worth 20 minutes
issues.preheader: HSA or FSA, the plan you actually use, and the beneficiary nobody updates.
issues.headline: Open enrollment in 20 minutes
explain: Open enrollment is the one time a year most people can change their health, dental and other benefits without a life event. It's easy to click "keep the same". Twenty minutes can be worth a lot more.

**HSA or FSA?** A Health Savings Account is only for people on a qualifying high-deductible plan; the money is yours and carries over year to year. A Flexible Spending Account is usually use-it-or-lose-it, though some plans allow a grace period or a small carryover. Your plan documents say which rules apply.
issues.tell: Check what you used this year before you choose next year. Last year's choice may not fit anymore.
steps: **Look back:** how many doctor visits, prescriptions or big bills did you have this year?
**Compare the total cost**, not just the paycheck deduction: premiums plus the deductible and what you'd pay out of pocket.
**Check the dates and details** in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}}, and ask {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}} anything that isn't clear.
quick_hits: **Using an FSA?** Plan for what you'll actually spend. Money left over may be lost.
**Update your beneficiaries** for life insurance and your {{RETIREMENT_PLAN}} while you're logged in.
issues.job: Write down how much you spent on health care this year, from your statements or insurer's app. Use it to compare plans.

lobby.headline: 20 minutes now, all year better.
bullets: Look back at what you used.
Compare total cost, not just premium.

social.caption: Open enrollment is here. Before you click "keep the same", look at what you used this year, compare the total cost of each plan, and check your HSA or FSA rules. Dates and details are in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}}. Questions? Contact {{BENEFITS_CONTACT}}.
social.alt: Money Made Simple at Work: open enrollment. 20 minutes now, all year better. Look back at what you used. Compare total cost, not just premium. Update your beneficiaries.

issues.topic: Holiday spending and buy now, pay later
issues.subject: Set your holiday number before the sales start
issues.preheader: One number for the season, and what to know before you split a purchase into four.
issues.headline: Set your holiday number
explain: The easiest way to avoid a January hangover is to decide on one number for the season before the sales begin: gifts, travel, food and all.
Buy now, pay later can feel like free money. It's still a loan. Several plans at once are easy to lose track of, and a missed payment can mean fees.
issues.tell: Decide what the holidays cost before the stores decide for you.
steps: **Pick your holiday number** and write it down. Divide it between people and events.
**Track it** in a note on your phone as you go.
**Using buy now, pay later?** Keep a list of every plan and payment date, and make sure the payments fit next month's budget.
quick_hits: **Start a holiday fund for next year** in January: a small amount each payday makes next December easier.
**Gift card or package text you weren't expecting?** It may be a scam. Don't click the link.
issues.job: Write your holiday number on a note in your phone today, before Black Friday.

lobby.headline: Pick your holiday number.
bullets: Decide one number for the season.

social.caption: This month: set your holiday number before the sales start. One amount for gifts, travel and food, written down and tracked. Using buy now, pay later? It's still a loan, so list every plan and payment date. {{EAP_LINE}}

explain: A few things have a December 31 deadline, and a few are just easier to do before the new year gets busy.
None of this takes long. Pick the ones that apply to you.
issues.tell: A little end-of-year tidying makes January easier.

**Raise your {{RETIREMENT_PLAN}} contribution** for the new year, even by 1%. {{MATCH_LINE}} The IRS publishes next year's contribution limits each fall.

quick_hits: **Moved or changed your name this year?** Update your address with payroll so your W-2 reaches you.

issues.job: Check your address in {{BENEFITS_PORTAL}} so your W-2 goes to the right place. It takes 2 minutes.
